editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The following oral history testimony is the result of an interview with Malone Hill Farrar on November 19, 2008, by Bobbie Ames in Pasadena, Texas. The interview was transcribed and processed by Bobbie Ames. The reader should bear in mind that she or he is reading a verbatim transcript of spoken, rather than written prose. Insofar as possible, this transcript tries to represent the spoken word. Thus, it should be read as a personal memoir and not as either a researched monograph or edited account. To the extent possible, the spelling of places, names, foreign words, and personal names have been verified, either by reference resources or directly by the interviewee. Some uncertainties will inevitably remain regarding some words and their spellings. In these scenarios a (ph) follows a word or name that is spelled phonetically.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Mr. Farrar, we are going to start your interview now. Are you ready to go and willing to participate?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes, willing to go.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. This is the interview of Malone Hill Farrar at the office of Ames Court Reporting and Video in Houston, Texas. The date is November 19th. It's approximately 2:00 o'clock. This is taken through the National Court Reporters Association for the Library of Congress, the Veterans History Project. Mr. Farrar, I'm very glad to meet you today. Would you mind stating your full name?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Malone Hill Farrar.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Thank you for coming out. We are going to start your interview. Would you tell me what squadron you were attached to?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, I was attached to -- during the war, to two or three different outfits. One of them -- the one I was in when the war started was Advanced Base Able was the name of the thing. It was in Norfolk, Virginia. And we were supposed to go to North Ireland, Northern Ireland, to set up a patrol plane base to help the British with the submarines in the North Atlantic.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. I was just trying to identify your unit.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: We are going to start from the very beginning. Where were you born?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was born in North Zulch, Texas.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: North?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Zulch, Z-u-l-c-h.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And your birthdate, please, sir?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The 20th of February, 1921.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So that makes you how old?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Eighty-seven.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Eighty-seven. You are remarkable; you drove out here and filled out the papers. What did your parents do for a living?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, my mother was just a housewife, and my daddy was a pharmacist.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: A pharmacist, right. Do you remember where you were on Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was in Banana River Naval Air Station, Banana River, Florida.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So you had already joined the service?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I had been in the service since January of 1940.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you think when Pearl Harbor happened?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I knew that we was into it, then.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And what did your mother and dad think?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, my mother died when I was seven years old. So...

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: My dad -- I was already in and I don't know what he thought, but I was the only one in the family that was in the service at the time.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Is that right? What made you want to join the service?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I joined the service, well, it was in the middle of the depression, and I was looking for a job and I couldn't find one. So, I joined the Navy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The Navy was your preference?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: All right. After Pearl Harbor, what happened to you?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, what happened to me, I was, like I say, in Banana River, went back to Norfolk. And by the way, when the war was declared, we had five airplanes, flying boats, down at Banana River. And each one of those flying boats had two 50-caliber guns. And they had also two 30-caliber guns. Each plane had this. And when it started, we were down there. We were actually based in Norfolk Virginia. But, we didn't have a round of 50-caliber ammunition to go in those planes. And they put us out to hunting submarines. And we got beer cans and threw beer cans if we saw any.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you see any?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. We never did see any.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Tell me exactly what is a flying boat?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: A flying boat, like a PBY or a PBM, a big flying boat with twin engines. Lands on the water.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Don't have any wheels; you have to put wheels on it after you -- if you want to get it out of the water.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, it just stays in the water?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Stays in the water all the time.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you said that your job was to go to Ireland. How did you get there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We didn't go to Ireland.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You didn't?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. That stopped the advanced base.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh! Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And they turned this outfit into a school, made it into a training unit and we started -- all of us started training mechanics.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Aviation mechanics at Norfolk. And I stayed at Norfolk for, oh, I guess, a year training mechanics. And then, I trained the second class of mechanics. I told my division officer, "I want to go with them when they go."

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you get your mechanic training?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: In the Navy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And then, you turned around and taught two classes?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Then, I turned around and taught two classes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And where did you go?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Ended up from Norfolk we went to -- they sent us out to California.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And then where?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Then we was all up and down the coast of Califoria because they were waiting on the war to which way they was going to go.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. What were you -- I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was at the Receiving Shift out there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Doing what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Mostly nothing. Working but there was thousands of people out there. Everything was crowded.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of people?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Navy and Army and Marines.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you said you went up and down the coast?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Doing what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Waiting?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Just waiting and they put us where we thought we could do the good, then.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Went to -- well, we started out in Sunnyvale, California at the airbase there. And then, the receiving ship at Goat Island.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: No, I meant when you went overseas, where did you go?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: When I went overseas?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We finally left the "states," and we went straight to New Caledonia. Noumea, New Caledonia.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Is that in the South Pacific?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It's in the South Pacific.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How did you get there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Boat. Ship.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Ship.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was the name of the ship?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The name of the ship, I forget. It was a liner.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Commercial?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: A liner they had confiscated from Moore McCormick Lines. I forget what it was called.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Like THE QUEEN MARY or something?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was THE PRESIDENT POLK, P-O-L-K.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was a President Liner.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How was the trip over?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, pretty good.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Anybody get seasick?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Everybody got seasick.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Everybody.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We had about two thousand men on there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Had you been on a ship before?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, I had been on a ship before.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you liked it?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was your job on the ship, mechanic?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. Just well, pulling targets for short-range battle practice.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. That was on the trip over to New Caledonia?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no. This was before that.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's actually what I was asking. Before that.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Before that, before the war started.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was at San Diego and we had to -- they put us on what they call a target repair party.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Didn't you just love San Diego?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The weather, I love it.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, it was. It was nice.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: On the ship going over to New Caledonia, you didn't have a job?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And there were 2,000 men on the ship, THE PRESIDENT POLK?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: At least 2,000.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you think about New Caledonia?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: New Caledonia was all right, but, there was 10,000 sailors down there. You know, and very few -- it was a French Colony.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. Did you know what you would be doing there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Waiting.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Waiting for the war to escalate?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. Now, while we there, we was there about -- we offloaded our boats. We had two ships. We offloaded everything from the "states" to New Caledonia, and we was waiting to move up. See, we were south of the Solomon Islands. That's where we ended up, at the Solomon Islands. But, while we were there, well, they got us all the aviation. We only had about twelve or fourteen aviation people. But, there was ready yeoman and metalsmiths and mechanics and all. And they got us out of the movie one night about 10:00.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: "Pack your bags, everything you need; be ready to go at 6:00 the next morning with everything that you've got." So we did. And next morning they put us on a truck and took us to the dock, loaded us into a motor launch, and we headed out the channel and while we were heading out the channel, one of the boats backed away from the dock and went with us and we threw our stuff on the ship. It was a destroyer. And we escorted us and -- another destroyer escorted two liberty ships.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Do you know the name of the destroyer?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, I don't -- yeah, THE BALLARD, B-A-L-L-A-R-D.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And did you know where you were going?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you go?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We were going to the Solomon Islands.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And we had to escort two liberty ships from Noumea to another island, which was Esporito. Esporito Santos.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was your MOS at that time, your job?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was still an Aviation Mechanic.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Aviation Mechanic.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How long did it take you to get to these places?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It took us four days to get to Esporito Santos.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you were on the destroyer?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What is a liberty ship?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: A liberty ship was -- they called them "Kaiser coffins." They welded them together and it's slow, 11 knots was as fast as they could go.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What is their job?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Hauling everything.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What happened when you got to the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, we didn't get to the Solomon Islands yet.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We stayed overnight at Esporito.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The next morning, just us by ourself, nobody else around us, we left early in the morning, and see, at Esporito we got behind the submarine nets. They had submarine nets. We could get back there and sleep tight without...

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You're talking about the 14 Aviation Mechanics?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I'm talking about the destroyer.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh! Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The destroyer got behind the nets.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Who left in the morning, the destroyer?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We did. The destroyer with us on it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: On your way to?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Guadalcanal.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: My goodness.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And all that day, by ourself, nobody around us, all day long, and then, all night and early the next morning, we could see the Solomon Islands from the ship. And they pulled in there, pulled in close to the beach about 200 or 300 yards from the beach. They had two boats on there. We put all our stuff in the two boats and got in the two boats and they dropped the boats in the water and the destroyer took off. And they took us to the beach and left us on the sandy beach there, and threw our stuff off on the beach. We got off. The boats went back out there and stayed until the destroyer -- the destroyer didn't slow up only long enough to pick up those boats. And then, as soon as he picked up these boats, he headed to another island over there that had a submarine net he could get behind.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: So, then, they took us I ended up -- well, this is part of the crew (indicating). Well, I've got a better picture than that and I identified all of them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was your rank at that time, Mr. Farrar?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was a First Class -- Wait a minute. No. I was a Chief Petty Officer.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. What do you go in the Navy as?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Apprentice Seaman.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So you had been promoted once or twice?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I had been promoted five or six times.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was E7.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How long had you been in?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I had been in less than four years.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You did well. So what did you do on the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: After we got there, they assigned me and most of these people here (indicating) assigned us to a squadron there. The problem they had there was fighter planes. They decided to assign us to a fighter plane squadron because what they'd do, the carrier wouldn't come within range of the thing. So, what they'd do, they'd launch all of the airplanes about three hundred miles out, and they were all one-man airplanes. Well, on the island, there was no mechanics; they had two mechanics taking care of 26 airplanes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: On the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. They were Fighter Strip No. 1 on there, the Henderson Field.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They were fighter planes?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Fighter planes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many man crew, one?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: One, just one pilot.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of planes?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Grumman, F-4F.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did they have a slang name? Like Thunderbolt or anything?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no, they didn't have nothing like that for it. Wildcat. Wildcat Fighter. Sure.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They had on there machine guns?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What else?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That's all, just machine guns. Six machine guns.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: On each plane?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: On each plane.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You know, some of them had cannons; I couldn't believe that.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I know they had some with canons.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I've learned so much on these interviews, Mr. Farrar.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We had -- well, the Army put together, the Army Air Force, put together some B25's with three-inch 75 millimeter guns, that big around. (Indicating) And they put them in them B25's. And they sent them up to -- they come up to us after we got up on into the islands, but, they didn't -- everybody was scared of them because when the first got into action, with the things, the first time one of them started in on a run, he would have been in position to fire this gun, and "whssttt," the plane exploded.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And killed everybody, you know. That was the end of that.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Outside the plane too?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah -- no, no. The Japs, they was shooting at the Japs.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: A Jap airfield, you see.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you said killed everybody. Who?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They had three or four people on a crew.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh! I thought you were still talking about the one-man plane.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. This is a bomber.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. Did you meet any of the pilots?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We knew most of the pilots.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was their average age?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The average age is about twenty-six, twenty-seven.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Twenty-four. A lot of young ones.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you lose many?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. The squadron that I was in there on Guadalcanal, when they left, they come back to the "states." They had lost two. The knew one was dead because they saw him crash, but the other one was just missing. But, after the thing come back, they found this fellow. He was out there in a one-man liferaft.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He sat out there 21 days on that ocean.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: But, the Solomon Islands, I'll bet there was a lot of shark activity out there.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, there's sharks in there. You could see them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: But, the Solomon Islands are spread out, aren't they?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They are long, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you travel in any other islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Other islands, yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Within the Solomon chain? Did they have sub names like --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Guadalcanal was a big island. That's the first one.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's part of the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, that's the south end of it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. What's another one?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Russell Islands and then, Bonica, and then, New Georgia.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You were naming some of the islands within the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yes. There was Bonica. Well, I was on New Georgia. Then, right across from us was Rendova. And just north of us was Vela Lavella.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go to any of those?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I went to one, yeah, on -- well, I didn't go to any of the other islands outside of flying over them and seeing people that worked over there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Were any of them occupied by the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: All of them were occupied by the Japanese.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yours, too?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. We went on that -- we left Guadalcanal and made a landing up on New Georgia. We took a Japanese airstrip away from them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The soldiers did, the 47th Infantry. And they -- and we come in behind them and the strip was a mess. Full of shell holes. The Japs couldn't use it. Dead Japs all over the place. And the Seabees come in there with us, a Seabee company. The Seabees has got about 1,200 men in a batallion, and they've got all kinds of equipment.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Wonderful?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And they started in --

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: -- did their job?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: -- and then, five or six days, they had an airplane landing there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did any of your squadron get killed?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: One man. Well, two or three of them, I guess.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Accidents or what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no. This man here (indicating) there is a picture of him. He's dead now.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What happened?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He got shelled. Japs moved a gun and started shelling us.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And he caught one of the first shells.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They were in the jungle; you didn't see them?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, we couldn't see them, no. They moved them in overnight and started shelling them late in the evening.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you have -- I don't want to sound ignorant, but, did you have watchouts, men who were --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We had Marines there. The Marines were there. We all had -- when we went on the island, we come from Guadalcanal and they put us off on a little bitty island right close by. And then, took us in small boats across the water over to where this airstrip was. And our skipper was with us. It was about 12 of us to begin with, and we all had hand grenades and rifle, ammunition, everything.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What is a skipper, the head of your --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The head of the outfit, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Why do you call him skipper; is he a Captain?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He was a Lieutenant Commander. He's the commanding officer.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Of your 14 men or of what? Commanding officer of what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Commanding officer of the unit, my unit.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many were in your unit?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, with the Seabee Battalion, it was about twelve hundred people. But, mainly just the aviation is where we went in. We went in first.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How old was he?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The skipper?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, skipper was about forty, I guess. He's a -- he graduated the academy, the Naval Academy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Do you remember his name?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Evenson.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you see any shark activity out there in those waters?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Sharks?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Sharks.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, we didn't. They don't come around. Deep water is all.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The reason I asked, there was so many Navy men lost to sharks.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That was in the Central Pacific.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Which is where most of them were.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Down in the islands like that, we didn't -- well, the Navy swam in there all the time, so...

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You know THE INDIANAPOLIS --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: -- when the Japanese sunk it, 800 some odd, and most of them were lost to sharks.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I had a story from one of the veterans about that.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: About THE INDIANAPOLIS carrying the atom bomb?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yep!

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I would like to ask you about --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They court martialed that skipper, too. The commanding officer.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Why was that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Because all of them men out. He wouldn't send a message.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He was under radio silence, and when the ship was sinking even, he wouldn't send a message, and that's what they got him on. But, I don't think -- I think it was completely uncalled for.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Hindsight is good, isn't it?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Do you recall anything humorous or funny that happened during your tenure overseas?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, it was comical, but I don't think it was funny too much, didn't know whether to laugh until it was over with, you know. But, I know one time when we were on our way down to Noumea, the officers, one of the officers on the ship, we had four 50-caliber -- 30 caliber -- 20 millimeter anti-aircraft guns. They had two on each side of this transport that we were on. So he wanted to have some practice, to have them, so he built a kite, and they worked two or three days and got that kite and got the thing, and when the wind was right, well, they put the kite out. The kite was a big kite; it was about five or six foot tall. And they got it out there and it was out about oh, I guess, 150 yards, and it was hanging out there. And when it got just right, well, this Lieutenant had everybody on the gun -- they had two guns on one side, told them two guns, "Start firing." The first round that come out of that gun hit that kite right smack in the middle and "whooff."

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Don't you know it?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It went in the water and that was it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many hours did it take him to build the kite?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, I don't know, a couple of days. That was funny. Everybody laughed about that.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Know any others you can recall?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, well sometimes in the foxhole, I know when the Japs are coming in bombing, I remember one time they laid a stick of bombs right down through our camp where we were.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Whow!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And everybody was asleep. This was about two o'clock in the morning. And when I woke up, everybody was under a mosquito net, too, everybody.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, everybody had to sleep under a mosquito net. And what I used to do when I went -- I would always take my shoes and tie the laces together so I wouldn't step on them. I kept the shoes under my cot. It was a cot, oh, that I slept on. And when I woke up, the siren wasn't even going off, but somebody hollered. I don't know who it was, but somebody made a noise and I woke up. And when I woke up, I could hear that Jap and he was right straight above us. Well, if he's straight above us, if he's dropped a bomb, they are just about on the way.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, I come out of there. We had a nice foxhole that we had built. And everybody out at the same time, and everybody made it to the foxhole.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yours?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yours was the best?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The bomb hit in the tree over my tent.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And it exploded, and it put shrapnel, the whole top of the tent looked like stars, see?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many men slept in a tent?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We had about six in this tent.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They had all got out of there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We all got out and got in the foxhole.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How deep was it?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I dug some of it out of the foxhole, too, pieces of it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How deep was the foxhole?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. We built it up like on the side of a hill, built it up with sandbags and everything.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many men would it hold?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It would hold about six and anybody else who wanted to get in. Many could get in there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Anybody die from that bombing?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Not that bombing. I don't think nobody got hurt at that bombing.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of plane would that be?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was a Japanese bomber. Bettys. They called them Bettys, B-e-t-t-y-s.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Are those bombs not 500 pounds?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no. These were 100 pounders.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, smaller bombs?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We called them daisy cutters, because if they hit down at Guadalcanal -- you could see where a bomb hit, and it would be in the big field. That grass down there was about five-foot high, and you would walk out there and there wouldn't be a piece of grass anywhere, but, there would be a hole, a little bitty hole, and they would have one bomb fin in it. The bomb fins were welded onto the case, and when that bomb exploded, it went in 50,000 pieces, and it was just like a mower, like somebody come in there and mowed it, and if you were sticking out of the hole that far, you got a piece of shrapnel.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Like a dirty bomb, huh?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was mean.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Do people get malaria in the Solomon Islands?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes, they did.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And what happened to them then, what hospital did they go to?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They had a big hospital at Guadalcanal. And then, each outfit had their own. We didn't have a hospital -- we had a hospital after we got settled, but, underway, before we grouped up, well, each one would have their own corpsman and everything, and their own stuff. And when they got to one spot, well, they would all move together, and everybody would work on everybody else.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: But, we didn't have any problem with that.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I took a nurse Sunday and she was in a hospital in New Guinea.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: New Guinea, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And she got malaria, also.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, you can get malaria.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And she had three more relapses since she came home.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Once you get malaria, you've got it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: She told me the names of the medicines and the name of the mosquito.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Adabert.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Exactly. You didn't get it, huh?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, I didn't get that. I always wore long sleeves at night. Always wore long sleeves and slept under a mosquite net every night.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was the scaredest you got, if you don't mind me asking?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Scaredest I got was that first night, the first night on that island. Because we got in there just about sundown, and there was about twelve of us. And the Army had already come in there and the Seabees had come in there, too, and the Marines, and everybody was there. And they built these tents. And when we got in there, well, we got into where -- after they put us in a boat and they took us over to this island, and when we got across the airfield, the airfield was a mess, well, we was back about a half mile off of the airfield away from it. And it was dead still. And dead like I say Japs all over the place. And when we crossed the airfield there, the Marines had a 90 millimeter or 155 millimeter shell; they were shelling the front, the front lines, which was about nine miles up ahead of us. But, that night they didn't tell us anything. They said, "Get in the tent, four in a tent and you lock that tent up, all except the door, and load your rifle and you watch that door. Don't get out. If you get out at night, you'll get shot for sure." So, anybody out walking at night, anybody that was out there in the open, it was pitch dark.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Because they were still in the jungle?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We didn't know where they were.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: See.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What if you had to go to the bathroom?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: You just went there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It didn't make any difference.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: See?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Nobody came, though?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no. Nobody came. We got daylight the next morning, and then, we went down -- we was helping the -- we were trying to build a tower, a control tower, for the airfield. And the Marines had also brought in a bunch of 40-millimeters for anti-aircraft, and we was helping the Marines, just wherever we could help. And then, after about four days, five days I guess it was, that's when the Japs moved a little gun in. They moved a 37-millimeter gun in, and started shelling, and one of the first shells hit the camp where we were. I wasn't at the camp at the time; I was down on the airstrip when it hit the camp. It didn't get nobody; it wounded a couple of people. But, it just blew a tent all to pieces, everybody had to run. And they had a mess tent set up there cooking and everything. They abandoned that, you know. And everybody, when they finally got to us, they told us to "Go by the dump and pick you up a bandolier of ammunition for your rifle, and some C-rations." Now, C-rations was cans. "And just hide yourself for tonight and come back in the morning." And that's what we did. The next morning was daylight and we was there, and long about 7:00 o'clock, they started shelling again. Well, I was in the position to where I had a hill between me and them. And they couldn't shoot over that hill, so I wasn't in too much trouble. But, then, when they started firing, they got this buddy of mine. That's the one that got killed.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: He was your good buddy?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Will you state his name.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Cooper. We had two Coopers in the outfit, "Big Cooper" and "Little Cooper."

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, how cute.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He was "Little Cooper."

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was his rank?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He was Second Class, I think at the time. Yeah, he was Second Class. Yeah, Second Class Petty Officer.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Some of the gentlemen as K-rations and some as C-rations.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: C-ration was two cans.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: One can had meat and beans, meat and vegetables, hash, meat and vegetable stew. The other can had hardtack, and hardtack is them old crackers, round crackers.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They had crackers in it, and then, they had -- some of them had lemonade which was foddered lemonade. And some of them had chocolate. And the rations that we had there, that was the C-rations. Two cans made supposed to be a meal. We'd eat them up and they eat all right.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Not much of a choice, though, huh?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no. And then, the K-rations come in a box and was supposed to be a meal, a meal for four people.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Breakfast, dinner and supper was the K-rations.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The same thing in all three?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, the same thing in all three of them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: No eggs and bacon?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no, no, no. You didn't have nothing -- no -- no eggs, anyway. And then, they had a D-ration.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: D-ration was a chocolate bar.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Hot dog!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Big, I mean you would have to cut it with a knife, thick wouldn't melt, nothing melted.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: It's good for you.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you do for R and R or did you not have any?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Didn't have any.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How long were you there steadily?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, after we got there and got the strip to running -- and by the way, the Japanese strip was about 3,500 feet long, and about, oh, maybe 100 feet wide, and of course, they had taxiways around there where -- when the Seabees left, they had two Seabee battalions. They had an Army engineer out there, and the three of them working, well, when I left there, the strip was 8,200 feet long and 350 foot wide.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Had they occupied the Solomon Islands at that point?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. They had it going.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: All of it?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They had control of all of it, see?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Because after about four months, we never even got an air -- we never got an air raid at all.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you see any animals while you were near the jungles?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. See they had sloths down there, what they call sloths.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They had sloths and they had snakes, too. They had some pythons.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oscelots, any oscelots?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I never did see any animal like that.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I used to live in Panama in the Army and they had sloths and oscelots and -- otters? Did you see any otters?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, we didn't have any. There is no running streams down there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's necessary.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That's the thing.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, after we finished that eight months, they sent us back to the Supply Depot at Bonica, and we picked up new equipment and went back over to the Dutch East Indies, went back over past New Guinea on up to the Biak Islands, B-i-a-k was the name of them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How far was that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That was about -- it was about a little over 700 miles from Admiralty Islands. Admiralty Islands was right on the Equator.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go on a destroyer again?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We was on a supply ship. As soon as we got there, we had to unload it. And they couldn't. The problem with unloading is there is no docks.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And the water was so deep they couldn't anchor. Water 100 feet out from the dock was 600 feet deep.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: But they didn't have a dock.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Didn't have a dock, no; you couldn't --

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So how did you do that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They stayed underway, and we'd take the stuff off the ship and drop it in a boat and the boat take it to the beach.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's slow, huh?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. Oh, it took us a month almost.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of people live in the Dutch Indies?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Dutch Indies, natives. Oh, you want to stay upwind.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I mean bad.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did they think about the Occupation?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, they were like kids.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They loved you all?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They were different than the ones in the Solomon Islands. The ones in the Solomon Islands, you know what they were?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They were all settlers, they had been.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Were they black or white or --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They were black.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did they think about the Americans?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, they thought the Americans was great.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Had the Japanese been in the Dutch Indies --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, the Japanese were there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So, the Americans routed them out?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So, the Americans routed them out?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Was there any R and R in the Dutch Indies?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: No!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No R and R anywhere.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you do there, airstrip?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We just did an airstrip, bomber strip mostly. We had 48 B-24 bombers on there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you go from there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: From there I flew back to the "states." I didn't fly back.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Went on a ship?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I flew back to the Admiralty Islands, and then, they put me on the ship.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What ship?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: THE CLYMER, C-l-y-m-e-r, was a troop transport.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. How many men on there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, quite a few.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The trip back, was it better than the trip going over?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, we almost didn't get back.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What happened?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, they took us out. I stayed there two weeks waiting on this transportation, and when they finally got transportation, they took us out there and put us on the ship that evening. We were supposed to get underway at 9:00 the next morning, and it was a big harbor, big lagoon, and must have had 50-75 ships in there, just as far as you could see. And that night, we spent the night on there, and the next morning -- they only serve two meals on a troop transport, breakfast and supper and that's all.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And so we went down and eat breakfast, me and the men I come back with, and we was sitting up on the No. 1 hatch. We were fixing to go. They already had their boats set in cradles and everything and had them strapped down and everything for going to sea. Well, we were sitting up -- well, actually, almost under one of them boats. And all the sudden, that ship jumped about three feet straight up.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And I turned my head to see from behind me. All I could see was fire. And then, the concussion.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, my!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It come and the ammunition ship blew up, four thousand tons of TNT.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The entire crew was lost?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, Lord, anybody on there didn't have a chance.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I think it was a little over a hundred, maybe two hundred men.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I was just getting ready to ask you about tragic things. That's tragic.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That was it. That was one of the worst. We had that one and we had another one that happened during all the fight that we had going on there right after we took over that island, Munda was where we were.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: "Munder?"

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: M-u-n-d-a was the name of it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It's quite a city now, I understand. I read in the paper a tsunami hit it. And the place at the time it didn't have nothing. It was a coconut plantation to start with.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So they rebuilt it good?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they rebuilt it good.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: American citizens?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes -- no. The New Zealanders rebuilt it. It belonged to New Zealand.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, they were wonderful people.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, they are, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: From what I've heard.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: They can tell you. I've got a story. That fighter squadron I was in, after I got back, I sit down and wrote everybody I could and got all the information that I could get and I've got the film in here (indicating). I brought the film from Washington and I made up a little book about 50 pages of the -- it was when the pilots came back off of the hop, well, they would tell what happened, see, who they shot down and all this.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And some of the guys got shot down and these natives would pick them up and hide them.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, how great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And one of the men in one of the stories, he told one of the pilots all day and all night on this land, they crossed this island, but they had to go through the jungle. And then, when they got to this next island they had to go around it because Japs were all over it. So the only way they could do is they put him in one of them dugout canoes; they had two of them, one in the front and they towed this one and they put palm fronds all over him. And they told him, "Don't make no noise."

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's a very interesting story.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. Now, then, they took off and they can paddle and not drip any water, see, real slow. Well, here is this pilot laying under there and you can just wonder what is going through his head.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's right. And his heart, pound, pound, pound.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The first thing he knows he hears these Japanese talking, and they are in there among them Japanese with this boat, him in the boat. And he's just, you know -- and finally they get right on through. They get right through and out the other side. They saved him. They got him back and put him on the ship, and he was --

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Do you remember his name?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. I've got his name in this --

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's all right. The Japanese would think that nobody had the guts to come right by them?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: See, I made up a book.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did any of the pilots name their planes?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Some of them did.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Any of the names funny or outstanding?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, not in that squadron. Most of the bombers is the ones that's got the ...

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of food did you have? Then, your ship took off for home after that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Huh? Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of food did you have onboard?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, good. We come back to Pearl. Now Pearl was the first place we had been back where it was actually civilization. That was the first place we had hit civilization since I left the "states" from California. We left the "states" from Port Hueneme in California.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. What about the bunks on the ship?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, good, no problem.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Were they like --

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Six high.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Six high?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Any of those swinging hammocks or anything?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: No?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I slept in a hammock once or twice while I was in the Navy. In fact, they gave me a hammock when I went through boot camp. I don't know what happened to it; I lost it somewhere.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Then you went from Hawaii to California?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Hawaii back to California. And then, I got 30 days leave and finally, I got a Chief Petty Officer's uniform. I didn't have a uniform down there; I had a baseball cap.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go home on the 30-day leave?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What stage was the war in at that time?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was -- Let's see. This would be Christmas of '44. They were in Okinawa; see, they just made the landing in Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The Americans?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. See, when I came back, when we come back to go back to the "states" come back to The Admiralty Islands, the Admiralty Islands was a big supply depot and they had a floating drydock there. And pretty well set up. And the Leyte operations had been -- see, this Leyte, L-e-y-t-e in the Phillipines, that was in the Philippines.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, when the Leyte operation was going on, some of those folks on that Leyte operation -- some of the people in the Army and Navy, too, I guess, they left the "states" on a troop ship. And when they got off the troop ship, they was in the middle of the biggest fight we ever had.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I imagine.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, it was mean. We lost -- well, we lost four carriers down there, four of those carriers. One of the cruisers come in at the Admiralty Islands and got in that drydock and they took 17 bodies off of that. They had a flooded compartment that got hit by a torpedo.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where were you when the Atom Bomb was dropped?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was in Houston, by golly.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Still in the service?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, I stayed in the service 20 years.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, I didn't... I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you think about the A-bomb?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, I thought that was the best. Anything, I'll tell you.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Most of your service after the war was where?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, after the war, was all over the world.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great!

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I went to training command after I got back. I was down in Pensacola, two years.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Still doing the aviation airstrips and all?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Bless your heart.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You retired as what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I retired as Chief Petty Officer. They called the ADC's. It started out with ACMM, see? Aircraft Machinist Mate.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where did you meet your beautiful wife?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Houston.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And what year did you marry her?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And she went all over the world with you?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, after the war.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you had children?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. I had two girls.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And they enjoyed the travels?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was your favorite place outside of our wonderful country?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We spent two years over in Morocco.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you like that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, that was nice.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Right between the wars when everything was -- we was over there from '48 until '50.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I almost went there. I was in Barcelona, and people told me now not to go, things have changed.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, in Morocco.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: That's what I understand. See, at the time we were over there, it belonged to the French. French run it. It was French Morocco. But, then, they turned it over to the Arabs, see.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you make any life-long friends in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And were you friends with them after the war?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And did you go visit them or they visit you anytime?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We had reunions.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: My outfit, I got into helicopters after I got back from Morocco, but, the people in my -- I was in the outfit when I was on Solomon Islands, I was in the ACORN 8, A-c-o-r-n, that stood for Airfield -- Let's see.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you say ACORN 8?

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: See, ACORN No. 8, Airfield Construction Operation and Repair Navy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So you were in during the Korean War also?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go to Korea?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was aboard ship then.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go anywhere around Korea?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We went over there on -- I never did get on land in there, but I was in the Task Force that was there.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What was your outfit called then?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was on THE USS ESSEX.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And part of what outfit, your unit?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I was in the Helicopter Unit.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I mean like the division?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: HU2 or HU1. HU1. We had the helicopters.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: But, like a squadron name or a number?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Squadron No. HU1. And the detachment, we were assigned to THE USS ESSEX.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you stayed on board the ship and your job was the same?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. We come under the ship and the ship told us what to do.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Like what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We were plane guard. We were flying as long as they were flying.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And if one of them went in the water, the pilot got out and we'd pick him up and bring him back to the ship.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: In what?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: In the helicopter.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Oh, how great. Did you lose very many?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. If they got killed on the crash, of course, we couldn't get them. I picked up one over in the Mediterranean. I went back to the Mediterranean after I come back from Morocco, and I picked up a guy over there, when he went off of the ship, he went right beside it. He don't know what happened, you know, but he went in the water, just like that (indicating) right by the side of the ship. And we went in. Me and that pilot was sitting back in the back where we could see it, and when he hit the water, well, we took off and tried to -- the ship was moving about 24 knots.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: In the helicopter?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: In the helicopter, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Well, in Morocco, where did you live?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: On the beach, a little beach settlement.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Military quarters?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Navy?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was Navy quarters.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And your wife and daughters were there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: The security was good and all of that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The security was good, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you do for R and R there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, we traveled; we went to different parts. We went to Fez, Meknes, Casablanca. Sometimes you go up to Gibraltar.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How do you spell Meknes?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: M-e-k-n-e-s.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And how was the food there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Good, delicious food.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Can you give me an example?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. The wine and the -- when they served steak, it was all cooked on charcoal; that's the only way they could cook. They didn't have gas.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What about milk, was it served cold or tepid?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: You didn't mess with milk.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Because it wasn't pasteurized.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Was it from cows and goats?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Cows mostly.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Cows.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: We never messed with it. My wife figured out for the kids, she got some condensed milk, you know, Pet Milk, and she concocted up with vanilla and some flavoring and spices and stuff. She concoted up a drink that the kids would drink.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What about the water?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The water was fine; we didn't have any problems with it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. Didn't have to have bottled water?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I'll bet you look back on that as a very interesting experience.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How long -- well, you were in the entire length of the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Any of the Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Into, well, yeah, when I was over there in Korea, we got in on the tail end of Korea. They was already talking about the Armistice then, the troops. So, they moved us. I was on THE ESSEX and they moved us down south and we went down there and we got messing around and got up in that muddy water from the Anaway River, messing around in there early in the morning.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did they challenge you or anything?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So the Vietnam War hadn't started but it was getting ready?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: It was still going on with the French. They were still fighting the French up at that place they call Din Ben Pfu. In fact, that's what we went in there for. We launched two photoplays planes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Can you spell that Dien Bien Phu?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: D-i-e-n B-i-e-n P-h-u, I think is the way it was.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: All the history books have got it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: So, your entire MOS or job was airstrips and air safety?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I spent my last nine years in a helicopter.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How old were you when you got out of the Navy?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Thirty-nine.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Thirty-nine? You were in how many years?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Twenty.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you do after that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I went to work as an aircraft mechanic.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I worked in Houston.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I worked at -- well, it's gone now. Andrau Air Park.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's out west?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. West side of Houston.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I worked there and I worked at the Municipal Airport over here.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Where is that?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Beechcraft.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: At Hobby?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: At Hobby.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: At Hobby.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you go to any of the reunions?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah, I went to see ACORN -- ACORN 8 never did have any; they never did get together. And I found out that ACORN 7 had reunions, and I started going to their reunions in, oh I guess, I forget when it was now. But, anyway, there was ACORN 7 and I knew a bunch of the people. And this man here (indicating) that is dead now, he was in the 8. He was there, too.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Anybody ever come to visit you at your home in Houston?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. A good friend of mine from Pensacola. I've known him since about 1950.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. He comes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How about did you go to any reunions overseas?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you join any VFW's or anything like that after the war?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No. I joined the Shrine.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: How many countries do you think that you visited as a Navy man?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, shoot, I don't know. All over the Pacific, I guess, even up to the North Pole, got up to the North Pole, the magnetic pole.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What countries around the North Pole to get there?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Canada, we went up through Canada.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Went all the way around Alaska and went back in. All we had to do was go 200 miles north and we could come in at New York.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you ever see the Aurora Borealis?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Isn't it beautiful?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: It's one of my favorite sights in the world.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: You can go crazy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you had two lovely daughters?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And they are successful?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, my oldest daughter, she got a -- this is in '91, she had a little boy, 7-year old boy and she got a blood disease.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Your daughter, she died?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes. Ten days it killed her with something that eat the platelets out of her blood.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They never did...

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And they tried everything in the world.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: They can't with my muscles either.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And the other daughter is okay?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: The other daughter, yeah. She went through high school in Houston, both of them went through high school. And my youngest daughter went to -- my oldest daughter was a singer, she loved to sing and she sang for a long time.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What kind of music?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Just singing. Singing anywhere.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Did you raise your grandson or did her husband raise him?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Her husband raised him, see, the husband remarried.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And your grandson is a fine man now?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: He's all right. He's in good shape now.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: But, my youngest daughter, she went to Southwest Texas. She's a Diagnostician for Speech Therapy.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: She's retired now. She's retired from the prison system. She ended up in the prison system.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: And she's got two boys.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Mr. Farrar, you've had a great life.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: I admire you and respect you. I appreciate you coming out here and talking with me; I've enjoyed it so much and I think you are in just great shape and you drove yourself out here.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You didn't even need an accompaniment.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And you have a Stars and Stripe baseball cap. I love that, too.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: You saw my big American flag out front?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: A friend of mine gave it to me.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Good. You are just so well off. I guess we'll conclude it unless you can think of anything. When you got back home, what did you think after WW2?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Well, I thought it was -- well, after I got back to Corpus Christi, that's where they sent me. They sent me to Corpus Christi after I got back. And I had a buddy that I went to school with here, him and his wife. I was with them when they got married and everything. Well, he -- I joined the Navy. I joined the Navy about a year ahead of him. He graduated. I quit. I quit school in the 11th grade.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: To join?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah. Because they only had 11 grades then, and I quit in 1938. And anyway, he went to Canada and joined the RCF before the war started, and then, when the war started, they give him a special order discharge and he come back to the "states" and joined the Navy as a rear-seat gunner and a dive bomber. That's what he wanted to do all his life, he wanted to be a dive bomber pilot.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: What did you think about the war when it was over?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, shoot, it was the greatest thing in the world.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: And what do you think about war in general?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: No, no, don't want to have no part of it. But the thing is it's got to be worth it. It's got to be worth it or else don't get into it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: When you hit the U.S. soil, you had a feeling of relief and joy?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah. You don't know what...

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Isn't it wonderful meeting people from around the world?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: All people are the same.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: I know it.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: It's the politicians, you know, that allow us to meet.

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Politicians get us in all the trouble.

sp.speaker: Bobbie Ames
sp.p: Okay. I really appreciate it again; otherwise, I wouldn't have got to meet you. I guess that concludes the interview?

sp.speaker: Malone Hill Farrar
sp.p: Just about.
